questions.question: Explain the full transmission chain from a repo rate increase to lower inflation, link by link, in your own words.
questions.expected_answer: The SARB raises the repo rate, making it more expensive for commercial banks to borrow; banks raise their prime lending rate; loans (home, car, credit) become dearer for households and firms; borrowing and spending are cut back; total demand in the economy slows, easing the pressure that was pushing prices up, so inflation drifts back toward the 3-6% band.

questions.question: Why is it a serious error to say the Minister of Finance changes the repo rate, and what single question protects you from this type of mistake?
questions.expected_answer: The repo rate belongs to the SARB, which is independent of government; the minister controls only budget instruments — spending and taxation. The protective question is 'whose hand is on this instrument?' — Reserve Bank means monetary policy, government budget means fiscal policy.

questions.question: Describe how you would classify any policy move as expansionary or contractionary, and apply your method to (a) a VAT increase and (b) a repo rate cut.
questions.expected_answer: Ask whether the move puts more money and spending into the economy (expansionary) or withdraws spending power (contractionary). A VAT increase makes spending dearer and leaves less in pockets — contractionary fiscal policy. A repo rate cut makes borrowing cheaper and encourages spending — expansionary monetary policy.
